prompt: With `loans` and `limit` both 3, which branch of the `if` chain in `Loans.java` ran?
hint: The first true condition wins.

choices.text: `may borrow`
choices.why: `3 < 3` is false, so that branch was skipped.

choices.text: `at the limit`
choices.why: Right: `3 == 3` is the first true condition, and the rest were never tested.

choices.text: `at the limit` and then `over the limit`, since `else` always runs too
choices.why: An `else` runs only when nothing above it did.

prompt: Under `with &&:` nothing was printed, and under `with &:` the method printed its line. Why the difference?
hint: Which operator looks at its right side when the left is already false?

choices.text: `&&` is not allowed with a method call on its right
choices.why: It is allowed; it just was not needed, because the left side settled the answer.

choices.text: `&&` stopped at the `false` on its left
choices.why: Right: that is the short circuit, and here it saved a call.

choices.text: The two conditions gave different answers
choices.why: Both were `false`, so neither printed `refused`; only the work differed.

choices.text: The method caches its answer after the first call
choices.why: It was called once in all, under `&`; nothing was cached.

prompt: `member` may be `null`. Which condition is safe?
hint: The left side must stop the right one.

choices.text: `member.equals("Bruno") && member != null`
choices.why: The `equals` runs first, on a possible `null`, and throws before the check is reached.

choices.text: `member != null & member.equals("Bruno")`
choices.why: A single `&` evaluates both sides, so `equals` still runs on `null`.

choices.text: `member != null && member.equals("Bruno")`
choices.why: Right: when `member` is `null` the left side is `false` and `equals` is never called.

choices.text: `member != null || member.equals("Bruno")`
choices.why: When `member` is `null` the left side is `false`, so `||` goes on to the right side and throws.

prompt: `if (loans > limit) fine = 5; System.out.println("fine charged");` written on two indented lines under the `if`, with no braces. With 3 loans and a limit of 3, what is printed?
hint: Indentation means nothing to the compiler.

choices.text: `fine charged`, with the fine still 0
choices.why: Right: only `fine = 5;` belongs to the `if`; the `println` always runs.

choices.text: Nothing, because the condition is false
choices.why: The condition only controls the first statement after it.

choices.text: A compile error about a missing brace
choices.why: It compiles; that is what makes the bug dangerous.

prompt: `String word = loans == 1 ? "loan" : "loans";` uses the ___ operator, an `if` that produces a value.
hint: It has three parts.

prompt: In `Shelf.java` the genre was `"poetry"` and two lines were printed, `shelf B` and `shelf C`. Why?
hint: What stops a classic `switch`?

choices.text: Both `case "poetry"` and `case "history"` matched the string
choices.why: Only one case matches; the second line came from running on past its label.

choices.text: There is no `break` after `case "poetry"`, so it ran on into the next
choices.why: Right: a case is a label, and the code ran down to the next `break`.

choices.text: The `default` ran as well, as it always does
choices.why: `default` printed nothing here; it runs only when no case matched.

prompt: Why can the compiler not warn about a missing `break` in a classic `switch`?
hint: Look at the second `switch` in `Shelf.java`.

choices.text: Because `break` is optional in Java and has no effect on what runs after a case
choices.why: It has an effect: without it the code runs into the next case.

choices.text: Because the compiler does not read the inside of `case` blocks
choices.why: It compiles every line of them, and would report any error inside.

choices.text: Falling through is also written on purpose, as in `case 6:`
choices.why: Right: both are valid, so it cannot tell which one you meant.

prompt: A classic `switch (missing)` was given a `null` `String` and threw `NullPointerException` mentioning `"<local4>"`, even after `javac -g`. Why is no name shown?
hint: What does the compiler do with a `switch` on a `String`?

choices.text: Because `-g` has no effect on a program run from source
choices.why: The second run was compiled with `-g` and run as a class, and still said `<local4>`.

choices.text: The variable that was `null` is a hidden copy the compiler made
choices.why: Right: the `switch` calls `hashCode()` on its own copy, which has no name to keep.

choices.text: Because the JVM hides variable names in exceptions for security
choices.why: It shows them when it has them: lesson 9's `jagged[1]` is an example.

choices.text: Because `missing` was declared without a type
choices.why: It was declared `String missing = null;`.

prompt: Which of these may be the value of a classic `switch`? Choose all that apply.
hint: Section 03 listed them.

choices.text: An `int`
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: A `String`
choices.why: Yes, since Java 7.

choices.text: A `double`
choices.why: No: floating-point values cannot be `switch`ed on.

choices.text: A `char`
choices.why: Yes: it is an integer type.

choices.text: A `boolean`
choices.why: No: use `if` for a yes or no.

prompt: In an arrow `switch`, what happens after the matching case's right-hand side runs?
hint: No `break` was written in `Fees.java`.

choices.text: It falls through to the next case unless there is a `break`
choices.why: That is the classic form; arrow cases never fall through.

choices.text: The `switch` ends
choices.why: Right: each arrow case runs alone.

choices.text: The `default` runs too, to supply a value
choices.why: `default` runs only when no case matched.

prompt: Inside a `default -> { ... }` block of a `switch` expression, how does the block give its value?
hint: Not `return`.

choices.text: `return 0;`
choices.why: `return` would leave the whole method, not the `switch`.

choices.text: `break 0;`
choices.why: `break` takes no value in Java.

choices.text: `yield 0;`
choices.why: Right: `yield` gives the value of the block.

choices.text: The value of the last statement, as in some other languages
choices.why: Java needs the value stated with `yield`.

prompt: `NoDefault.java` covers `"book"`, `"magazine"` and `"dvd"` and has no `default`. Why does it not compile?
hint: What would the expression return for `"map"`?

choices.text: A `switch` on a `String` must use the classic form
choices.why: `Fees.java` used an arrow `switch` on a `String` and compiled.

choices.text: A `switch` expression needs a value for every possible input
choices.why: Right: there are endless other strings, so a `default` is needed.

choices.text: Two constants in one `case` need a `break` between them
choices.why: `case "book", "magazine"` is the arrow form's way to share a case.

prompt: `case Integer i -> ...` is written above `case Integer i when i > 100 -> ...`. What does the compiler say, and why?
hint: Cases are tried from the top.

choices.text: Nothing; both cases are chosen for 250
choices.why: Only one case runs, and the compiler refuses this order outright.

choices.text: That `when` is not allowed after `Integer`
choices.why: `when` worked on `Integer` in `Fees.java`; only the order was wrong here.

choices.text: That the guarded case is dominated: the first matches every `Integer`
choices.why: Right: it could never be chosen. Put the guarded case first.

prompt: Match each call to what `describe` returned.
hint: The cases are tried from the top.

prompt: A member's genre decides a shelf, and the code must not fall through by accident. Which form do you write?
hint: One form cannot fall through at all.

choices.text: A classic `switch`, with a comment on each `break`
choices.why: A comment does not stop the next person from deleting a `break`.

choices.text: An arrow `switch`
choices.why: Right: arrow cases never fall through.

choices.text: A chain of `if` statements without `else`
choices.why: Without `else`, more than one `if` can run, which is falling through by another name.

prompt: Put these cases of a `switch (o)` in an order the compiler accepts and that gives each its own inputs.
hint: Specific before general; `default` last.

prompt: `int day = 7;` runs through `switch (day) { case 6: case 7: System.out.println("closed"); break; default: System.out.println("open"); }`. How many lines are printed?
hint: Jump to the label, run to the `break`.

prompt: `if (loans = 5)` does not compile. What is the message, in substance?
hint: An assignment's value is the value assigned.

choices.text: That `=` cannot appear inside the brackets of an `if` condition
choices.why: It can; the problem is the type of what it produces.

choices.text: That an `int` cannot be converted to `boolean`
choices.why: Right: Java never treats a number as true or false.

choices.text: That `loans` might not have been initialised
choices.why: `loans` was set to 3 on the line before.

prompt: A program must handle a `String` that is sometimes `null`, with a different message for each of three values and for `null`. Which is the shortest correct version on Java 25?
hint: One form takes `null` as a case.

choices.text: A classic `switch`, which treats `null` as `default`
choices.why: A classic `switch` on `null` throws `NullPointerException`, as section 03 showed.

choices.text: An arrow `switch` with only a `default` for the `null` case
choices.why: Without `case null`, a `null` still throws before any case is tried.

choices.text: An arrow `switch` with `case null` and a `default`
choices.why: Right: since Java 21, `case null` is a case like the others.

prompt: In a `case Integer i when i > 100`, the condition after `when` is called a ___.
hint: It protects the case.
